manual_retrieved_paragraphs.text: We observed that three blocky pepper accessions carried the C. chinense-derived haploblocks in Chr11, whereas none of the other C. annuum accessions possessed these haploblocks (Fig. 5e). Intriguingly, within these haploblocks, we identified a CC-NBS-LRR gene named L, known to confer resistance to Tobamovirus spp.52. The L gene introgressed from C. chinense was the L3 allele, one of the four known alleles (L1–L4). The L3 allele has been validated to mediate resistance against the P0, P1 and P1,2 pathotypes of pepper mild mottle virus (PMMoV)53–55. Non-pungency is one of the most important traits of sweet blocky peppers. In the genomic region of the well-known Pun1 gene, we observed a blocky-pepper-dominant haploblock. Pun1 encodes a key enzyme in capsaicin biosynthesis, and a loss-of-function mutation in this gene results in non-pungent peppers56. This blocky-pepper-dominant haploblock existed at a low frequency (19%) in the ancestral and landrace accessions of C. annuum. Although this haploblock was nearly fixed in all blocky peppers, the Pun1 deletion genotype was consistently present in sweet blocky peppers but absent in pungent blocky peppers (Fig. 5h).This suggests that the inheritance of this haploblock from ancestral C. annuum accompanied the formation of blocky pepper, while the selection of the non-pungency trait for sweet blocky peppers led to the widespread presence of the Pun1 deletion allele in this haploblock (Fig. 5i).
